title: Latency tail & cost fingerprint — INT8/FP8/GPTQ kernel comparison
content:
Summary:

This is a working note capturing results from a targeted profiling sweep comparing quantization formats and kernel implementations with an emphasis on tail latency (p95/p99/p999) and an operational "cost fingerprint" for token-level inference. The goal is to produce actionable knobs for production rollouts (routing, fallback, autoscale signals) and to identify hotspots where kernel fallbacks or format conversions create disproportionate tail latency and cost.

High-level takeaways (short):
- INT8 specialized kernels give the best median throughput on A100 but show a heavier p99/p999 tail under mixed concurrency due to occasional kernel serialization and memcpy churn.
- AWQ builds are fastest for short sequences and aggressive batchshapes; however, we observed a reproducible stability blip (softmax logits variance) on a small subset of prompts vs GPTQ — needs eval set triage.
- FP8 paths give more predictable latency tails because they avoid falling back to slower reference kernels for certain ops, but at the cost of slightly higher average compute time vs best-case INT8 kernels.
- Kernel fallback events (quant->fp conversion, blocked GPU kernels) map tightly to p999 spikes; these are often caused by CPU-side packing/unpacking and lazy weight reprojection.

Experiment matrix (short):
- Models: Llama-2-13B-chat, Mistral-7B, in one case Llama-2-70B (smoke).
- Quant variants: INT8 per-channel (our fast matmul kernel), AWQ-4bit/8bit variants, GPTQ-4bit, FP8-e4m3 and FP8-e5m2 profiles.
- Kernels: fused_gemm (vendor), quant_matmul_fast (in-house), fallback_reference (slow path), awq_special (AWQ-optimized), fp8_streamlined.
- Hardware: A100-80GB (prod), H100-80GB (dev), T4 (edge smoke).
- Workloads: chat-like (rolling short prompts, 16-128 tokens), long-context generation (512/1024 tokens), and synthetic degenerate prompts (repetitive tokens to test KV cache and mem pressure).
- Concurrency shapes: single-request, 4x concurrent, 16x concurrent; batching windows 0ms/20ms/50ms.

Measurement methodology:
- Measure latency percentiles per-token and end-to-end generation; use p50/p90/p95/p99/p999.
- Capture kernel-level traces (NVIDIA CUPTI + our runtime trace) and mark kernel start/stop, memcpy events, and quant-conversion ops.
- Record fallback flags: "quant_fallback", "format_conversion", "kv_cache_miss", "cpu_serialize".
- Cost fingerprinting: compute tokens/sec * instance_cost to yield $ per 1M tokens. We normalize to the A100 on-demand hourly rate used in our infra chargeback (example numbers below).

Representative numbers (median of 10 runs, warm cache unless noted):
- Llama-2-13B, 32-token prompt -> 128-token gen, batch=1:
  - INT8 (quant_matmul_fast): p50=42ms/token, p95=85ms, p99=190ms, p999=420ms; cost_est_per_1M_tokens ~ $9.8 on A100.
  - AWQ (awq_special): p50=34ms, p95=70ms, p99=160ms, p999=380ms; cost_est_per_1M_tokens ~ $8.1 (but see quality note).
  - GPTQ (quant-gptq path): p50=48ms, p95=92ms, p99=210ms, p999=430ms; cost_est_per_1M_tokens ~ $11.2.
  - FP8 (fp8_streamlined): p50=46ms, p95=82ms, p99=170ms, p999=260ms; cost_est_per_1M_tokens ~ $10.4.

Observations and root causes:
- p999 spikes are almost always aligned with: (1) CPU-side weight packing for certain kernels, (2) synchronous memcpy between CPU<->GPU during format conversion, or (3) kernel serialization when the scheduler decides to run a fallback_reference kernel.
- AWQ path used a specialized CUDA kernel that avoids expensive packing at generation time; this explains the lower median. However, in ~0.3% of prompts AWQ logits diverge and downstream eval metrics (BLEU/ROUGE/QA EM) drop by 1–2 points. Need focused eval bucketization to understand prompt shape.
- FP8 path avoids the reference kernel in many ops because it keeps data in a compatible layout; this reduces tail but increases average time vs INT8 best-case because the FP8 kernels are not as highly optimized for GEMM throughput on A100 (future work: kernel fusion + tensor core tiling).
- GPTQ's memory layout requires occasional reorder that runs on CPU if memory pressure is high — causing long tails under 16x concurrency tests.

Why this matters for production decisions:
- SLOs: If customers require p99 < 200ms for chat, INT8 can hit median but p99/p999 may exceed SLO under load spikes. That suggests promoting FP8 or AWQ for higher-tier customers or routing to Dedicated capacity where concurrency is controlled.
- Cost vs reliability: AWQ gives attractive cost per token but needs quality gating; could be used as a canary route with automatic fallback to GPTQ if eval metrics drift.
- Autoscaler signals: Kernel-fallback flags are an early indicator of saturation; surface these as metrics to the scaler to trigger more headroom before latency SLOs are violated.

Micro-ops and short-term fixes we validated:
- Prepack weights at model load time (measured elimination of pack-on-first-request p999 spike).
- Pin and preallocate host->device staging buffers for format conversions to avoid dynamic cudaMalloc/cudaFree jitter.
- Add a tiny async conversion worker pool to convert occasional GPTQ/INT8 weight pages off the hot path; reduced observed p999 by ~30% in 4x concurrency test.

Quality verification notes:
- We ran a 5k prompt eval set across buckets (instruction style, code, math, conversation) comparing AWQ->GPTQ->FP8 outputs. Binary pass rate: AWQ passed 94.6% of prompts vs GPTQ baseline (some drop concentrated in code/math). Need decomposed hypothesis: AWQ's per-channel scale heuristic may under-quantize rare-value heads.

Open questions / TODOs:
- [ ] Re-run AWQ with alternative folding parameters on the code/math prompt bucket and measure deltas.
- [ ] Implement an async weight reformatting daemon to see if we can remove CPU fallback entirely for GPTQ conversions.
- [ ] Prototype fused FP8 GEMM kernel with 64x64 tiling for A100 and re-run the long-context test.
- [ ] Add kernel-fallback metric to routing policy and test canary routing with auto-fallback to GPTQ for a small customer cohort.

Actionable recommendations (for next 2 sprints):
- Short-term: Ship prepack-at-load and pinned staging buffers across all quant formats (low effort, high impact).
- Mid-term: AWQ can be a discounted route only behind quality gates; build prompt-bucket evaluator and rollback automation.
- Long-term: Invest in FP8 fused kernels and async weight reformatting — these reduce tails and make tradeoffs easier for customers.

Notes-to-self and references:
- See trace artifacts: /traces/2024-04/awq-vs-int8-run-14 (internal).
- Related PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/876 (kernel pinning + prepack)
- Jira: ENG-4321 (quant format async daemon research)

If we decide to promote AWQ as a canary route we must pin a rollback condition: p99 latency > 250ms or quality drift > 1.0% vs baseline on the monitored eval-set.
